title: When friends drift
description: Some friendships end with a bang, but most end with a long, quiet tide going out — and it is not always anyone’s fault.

body.heading: Drift is not betrayal
paragraphs: New cities, new partners, new jobs, new babies: lives change shape, and friendships fitted to the old shape strain. It is tempting to read drift as rejection, but usually it is just logistics wearing an emotional disguise.
Holding that thought loosely — “we have drifted” rather than “I have been dropped” — saves a great deal of unnecessary pain.

body.heading: One honest attempt
paragraphs: If the friendship matters, make one clear, unembarrassed attempt: “I miss us. Can we find a rhythm that fits your life now?” Sometimes the answer reopens everything. Sometimes it confirms the tide — but you will never wonder whether one sentence could have changed it.
Make the attempt without a bill attached. “After all I’ve done” turns an invitation into an invoice, and invoices are easy to decline.

body.heading: Let some go with thanks
paragraphs: A few friendships are for a season, and their ending does not erase their truth. You can be grateful for what a friendship was and still let it become past tense. Both things fit in the same heart, given time.
And tides, occasionally, come back in. People reappear after years as if no time passed. Leaving the door unlatched costs nothing.

takeaway: Read drift as logistics before rejection, make one honest attempt, and let the rest go with thanks.
